fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years has ushered in a new twist to the already unusual relationship between President Donald Trump and the world’s most powerful central bank.

Trump raised eyebrows on Wednesday evening by appearing to suggest that he gave Kevin Warsh, his handpicked Fed chairman, permission to raise rates – even though it was the “wrong” move. The president implied that Warsh had no choice but to embrace a rate increase because the Fed chief was outnumbered on the “hostile” rate-setting committee he oversees.

“I talked to Kevin and I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter…I said, ‘Do what you want because it doesn’t matter’ because he doesn’t have the votes,” Trump told reporters.

The remarks raise plenty of questions about how much – if at all – Warsh is consulting with a president who has been willing to cross red lines in his quest for dramatically lower interest rates.

Those questions are especially sensitive because the Fed is designed to be insulated from the political winds in Washington. Central bankers are required to make trillion-dollar decisions on whether to raise or lower interest rates based on what’s best for the economy, not for the political party in power.

Tellingly, some Fed watchers and former officials reacted to the remarks with disbelief.

“It’s an unusual and unfortunate comment to make. Clearly, the Fed chair does not need the president’s permission to raise rates,” Eric Rosengren, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, told CNN on Thursday. “The implication is that the chair got a hall pass. I have no idea how truthful the comment was.”

Krishna Guha, vice chairman and head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI who criticized Warsh’s initial stumbles, dismissed Trump’s claims.

“The market believes – and with good grounds – that Kevin Warsh owned this decision and that the committee was strongly united behind him,” Guha said. “There is no evidence here or to the market at large that Warsh was dragged into this by colleagues – or permissioned by the president.”

The risk is that Trump fuels suspicions that swirled on Wall Street this summer that Warsh may not be truly independent. That’s dangerous because a Fed doing the White House’s bidding could lose control of market-set interest rates, dramatically increasing the cost of mortgages and car loans. And a loss of faith in Fed independence could unhinge inflation expectations among investors and consumers.

The Fed declined to comment to CNN about Trump’s remarks.

For his part, Warsh tap-danced around questions related to the man who nominated him.

“I’m not a Wall Street newsletter. Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street,” Warsh said during the press conference on Wednesday. “We’ll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them.”

Asked by a reporter when he last spoke with the president, Warsh said: “I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president.”

Tim Mahedy, CEO and chief economist at research firm Access/Macro, said he found that response from Warsh “strange.”

“The right answer is, ‘I didn’t talk to the president.’ I don’t think the president is talking to Warsh beforehand. That would be shocking,” said Mahedy, a former official at the IMF and San Francisco Fed.

The other risk is that, intentionally or not, Trump diminishes Warsh as an ineffectual leader – just as he appeared to be starting to find his footing.

“It makes it seem like Warsh has no control over this committee, like he was completely ineffectual in convincing his colleagues,” said Mahedy.

Warsh emerged from the meeting looking independent. Not only did he preside over a rate hike the White House did not want, but he explained it clearly and with the unanimous support of his colleagues – including former Fed Chair Jerome Powell.

“It felt like the day the Fed became Warsh’s Fed,” Evercore’s Guha said. “He was a lot more assured, coherent and credible yesterday. What he’s saying basically adds up.”

But now if Warsh and a majority of his colleagues on the committee decide against a rate hike, he will face questions about whether the president put his finger on the scale.

In the past, most presidents have gone out of their way to even avoid the appearance of interfering with the Fed because it was widely accepted that an independent Fed builds confidence.

None of this is to say Trump unleashed on the Fed in a way that would have unnerved investors. In fact, Trump’s initial reaction to the first rate hike under Warsh was relatively mild, especially compared with his relentless and deeply personal condemnation of Powell, his last handpicked Fed chair.

While Trump bashed Warsh’s colleagues as “very hostile” and “very political,” he singled out the Fed chief for praise. “He’s a good man, Kevin Warsh,” Trump said.

“People were fearful of a fierce backlash from the president against this decision to raise rates and a resumption of the conflict between the White House and the Fed,” Guha said.

Of course, the Warsh-Trump relationship will continue to evolve, likely guided by what happens next to inflation, borrowing costs and the path of the S&P 500 and all-important Treasury rates.

Mahedy said he worries that the relationship will break down if the Warsh-led Fed continues to raise rates – as many suspect it will be forced to.

“It’s not hard to see more blame being put on the Fed and Warsh – and then it will start to look a lot like Powell,” said Mahedy. “It’s kind of a train wreck – but a slow-moving one.”

fullText:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday evening said he counseled Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh to vote for an interest rate hike because other Fed officials were expected to vote that way anyway.

"I said do what you want because it doesn't matter because he doesn't have the votes," Trump said to reporters as he was traveling in North Carolina to campaign for a Senate candidate.

"I told Kevin, I said, 'You might as well vote with the board because it's just not going to matter. ... The board is very hostile," Trump said. "They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing. They're a bunch of politicians. They are people put on by politicians."

In the same interview with reporters, Trump also suggested that he doesn't expect Warsh to follow his directions, saying he wanted the Fed "to be independent."

The comments came after Federal Reserve officials voted unanimously to increase interest rates by a quarter point for the first time in three years, a move Trump decried on social media hours after the announcement.

Trump's account that he counseled the Fed chair on his vote was not confirmed by Warsh or other evidence. Asked at a news conference about Trump's repeated demands that Fed officials lower rates, Warsh declined to comment.

"I've got nothing for you on the discussion with the president," Warsh said, moving on to say the decision to raise rates was in fulfillment of the Fed's duty to the American people.

The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House, setting interest rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure. That independence has long been considered a cornerstone of the central bank's credibility - and a source of tension with some presidents, especially Trump, who wants dramatically lower borrowing costs.

Over the years, Trump has made clear he wants a central bank more responsive to his political agenda, pressing for steep rate cuts to ease the cost of financing swelling deficits and exploring options to oust board members appointed by Democrats.

Past administrations have also pressured the central bank, whose independence rests both on federal law and on norms that most recent presidents have been reluctant to test. Top aides to President George H.W. Bush publicly pushed Fed Chair Alan Greenspan to cut rates before the 1992 election. President Joe Biden met with Fed Chair Jerome H. Powell in the White House in May 2022 to show concern about inflation (though Biden stressed that he respected the Fed's independence).

While it's not unusual for presidents to meet with Fed chiefs from time to time, Trump's comments suggested a closer relationship.

A Fed spokesperson did not immediately return a request seeking comment about the conversation between Trump and Warsh.

Warsh, a Fed governor from 2006 to 2011, returned to the central bank in May, after a year in which Trump pressured the Fed in ways without modern precedent. Trump repeatedly criticized Powell, Warsh's predecessor, for refusing to bring rates down; he tried to remove Fed governor Lisa Cook; and he endorsed a Justice Department criminal investigation of Powell. Trump in January chose Warsh to fill the chairman's seat occupied by Powell, who has stayed on at the Fed as a governor. The Justice Department probe was closed.

The Fed's move Wednesday was seen by analysts as bolstering the central bank's credibility after concern that Warsh, who was nominated to the position by Trump, would not do what it took to get inflation under control.

Trump said the Fed board raised interest rates out of hostility toward him.

"They're raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as he can possibly do," the president said. "The problem they have is that we have the greatest economy in history."

title: House speaker sends lawmakers home early ahead of midterm election recess
description: The speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, speaks to reporters at the US Capitol on 16 September 2026 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty...
fullText:
The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess.

The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence.

It's the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday.

"I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis," the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch.

Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump.

"We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI," Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. "Because then we will lose our edge to China, and ​that has serious national security implications for every American family."

More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards.

In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker's latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes.

Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because "the House has done its work". Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election.

"You've seen the statistics we've been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention.

However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes.

Johnson also addressed Massie's impeachment resolution, calling it "a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention". The House speaker insisted it would be "immediately" postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts.

Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie's resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

fullText:
One day after a dramatic meeting of the arts institution’s Board of Trustees, during which members – many of whom are allies of President Donald Trump – voted to close its doors, lights inside the Kennedy Center’s main building appeared to have been turned off.

The doors had been locked at 6 p.m. Tuesday night and bike racks were stacked up by entrances to block public access.

But officially closing the public monument would violate a court order requiring it remain open as a lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty continues.

On Wednesday, US District Court Judge Christopher Cooper, in response to an appeal for an emergency hearing filed by Beatty, ordered the Trump administration to answer questions over the status of the building by Thursday at 10 a.m. ET.

Beatty issued the request after a member of her legal team was denied entry to the main building and “was informed by several security staff members that the building is currently closed to the public,” her attorneys said in a court filing.

A spokesperson for the Kennedy Center told CNN the building was “temporarily” closed due to safety concerns. But Beatty’s lawyers said that when they asked for an explanation from the Justice Department, they did not receive a reply – a violation of the court order, they contend.

When CNN visited on Wednesday, no signage was visible indicating any change of status to the main building – despite the fences and barricades over the doors.

A few security guards were outside as construction crews worked outside the building, where a fence with white curtains had been erected.

Outside the main building, the digital advertising boards still hype upcoming shows, and a landscaper was pruning the hedges. Employees came and went through a parking garage entrance. One of them told CNN that their badge worked for getting into the building – but only on the side doors.

A lone protestor stood outside with a sign that said: “There is still an injunction, remember?” And “shame on the Trump board.”

The relative calm of the scene at the center belies the drama that is expected to continue in the days to come.

The Justice Department has said it plans by Friday to appeal the court’s decision forcing it to remain open, while Trump has warned that the center may not reopen unless his name can be affixed to the building.

Trump later Wednesday seemed to raise the stakes if that effort fails: “It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”

Trump argued that his administration “should be recognized” for taking on the financial burden of fixing what he called “a mess.”

“For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition,” he told reporters.

Meanwhile, an annex of the Kennedy Center, a separate arts space known as The Reach, remains open.

On Wednesday, the song “Jolene” was being played. A Dolly Parton celebration is planned for September 25.

When asked if it will remain open, a worker there replied, dryly: “We have no idea.”

title: US Senate panel approves bill to bar government officials from pressuring networks on free speech
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 16 (Reuters) - The U. Senate Commerce Committee approved legislation on Wednesday to bar government officials from pressuring private companies to censor speech, citing threats from t...
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 16 (Reuters) - The U.S. Senate Commerce Committee approved legislation on Wednesday to bar government officials from pressuring private companies to censor speech, citing threats from the Trump administration ‌against late-night talk shows as evidence of efforts to stifle free expression.

The measure would allow citizens to ‌sue federal employees who pressure private companies into suppressing speech protected by the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which guarantees free expression. Both ​Republicans and Democrats on the committee said the bill was needed to curb government overreach.

The committee approved the bill 18-10. It must still pass the full Senate, where it is unclear when it may be taken up, and the U.S. House of Representatives to become law.

Senator Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the panel, said the bill, if it had ‌been in effect, would have allowed Disney-owned ⁠ABC's late-night show host Jimmy Kimmel to file suit after Federal Communications Commission chair Brendan Carr last year pressured station owners to stop airing Kimmel's show following remarks about ⁠the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

Senate Commerce Committee chair Ted Cruz cited actions by the administration of then-President Joe Biden that he said were intended to pressure private companies to censor speech protected by the First Amendment. He said ​the Biden ​administration sought to pressure Big Tech firms into "canceling Americans who ​spoke out against vaccine mandates and election ‌fraud."

The American Civil Liberties Union said the bill would have prevented Carr "from threatening the broadcast licenses of television stations that continued to air Jimmy Kimmel's show after he made remarks the White House did not like."

U.S. President Donald Trump has called repeatedly for ABC to lose its licenses over programming he dislikes. The reviews were ordered in April a day after Trump urged ABC to fire Kimmel.

Trump this month called for the FCC to rebuke or punish Comcast-owned ‌NBC's journalist Kristen Welker after she noted that the Republican ​president's success in endorsing political candidates has been mixed.

Last year, Cruz ​sharply criticized Carr days after he threatened the ​licenses of Disney and local broadcasters, saying Carr's comments were "dangerous as hell."

"I got to say ‌that's right out of 'Goodfellas'," Cruz said, evoking the ​Martin Scorsese gangster movie. "That's right ​out of a Mafioso coming into a bar going, 'Nice bar you have here. It would be a shame if something happened to it.'"

Disney and a spokesperson for Carr did not immediately comment.

Carr in April ​ordered early review of licenses for ‌the entertainment giant's eight company-owned ABC stations even though they were not scheduled to be considered ​before October 2028. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years ​before April.

title: US import prices jump in August on strength in capital, consumer goods
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 16 (Reuters) - U.S. import prices surged in August amid solid increases in the costs of capital and consumer goods, suggesting inflation could rise further in the coming months.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 16 (Reuters) - U.S. import prices surged in August amid solid increases in the costs of capital ‌and consumer goods, suggesting inflation could rise further in ‌the coming months.

Import prices rebounded 0.7% last month after declining by 0.3% for ​two straight months, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Wednesday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, would rise 0.4%.

In the 12 months through August, import ‌prices soared 7.0%, the ⁠largest increase since August 2022, after advancing 6.1% in July. The government last week reported accelerations ⁠in consumer and producer prices in August.

Higher inflation because of the oil price shock stemming from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and larger-than-expected ​nonfarm payroll ​gains in August are expected ​to push the Federal ‌Reserve to raise interest rates later on Wednesday.

Imported capital goods prices increased 0.9% last month after rising 1.0% in July. Prices for nonelectrical machinery gained 1.2% for the second straight month in August. An artificial intelligence spending boom is driving up prices ‌for imported capital goods.

Prices for imported ​consumer goods, excluding automotives, rebounded 0.5% ​after two straight monthly ​decreases. The cost of imported automotive vehicles, parts ‌and engines was unchanged.

Prices of imported ​fuel slipped ​0.1%, declining for a third straight month. Imported food prices edged up 0.1%. Excluding food and fuels, import prices ​jumped 0.8% after rising ‌0.3% in July. The so-called core imported inflation increased ​5.6% in the 12 months through August.

title: The real reason why Donald Trump is so furiously against AI guardrails
description: Washington’s biggest question this week: Why is President Donald Trump is so furiously against an AI slowdown in the wake of apocalyptic warnings from some top industry executives?
fullText:
Washington's biggest question this week: Why is President Donald Trump so furiously against an AI slowdown in the wake of apocalyptic warnings from some top industry executives?

The clue is in one word — "hoax" — that he's using to ridicule fears that computerized agents could one day seek to destroy humanity.

When Trump reaches for the H-word, two things are usually happening: He's facing a controversy threatening his political or personal priorities, and he's lost control of the politics.

Trump has long dismissed climate change as a "hoax." So it was a tell that he went on social media to specifically draw an analogy between a planet that is warming despite his denials and the calls for AI controls expressed by leaders in the industry.

The Jeffrey Epstein saga is a "Democratic hoax," according to Trump. Searing testimonies from the accused sex offender's victims make this a ridiculous charge. But Trump wants to end the storm over his onetime friend that periodically trips up his administration.

The same is true of another supposed "hoax": the investigations into the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021. The outrage was the culmination of another event Trump wants America to forget: his bid to overturn the 2020 election. The hoax routine worked — it got him back to the White House to wield expansive executive power.

The president seems to hope that by simply branding fears of runaway AI as a hoax, he can make them go away.

One of a president's jobs is to counsel a fearful nation, to examine and explain threats, and to advise whether a national effort must be summoned. "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself," Franklin Roosevelt said at the start of a presidency deep in the Great Depression.

Every commander in chief followed suit in the Cold War. And George W. Bush corralled the country after 9/11, almost exactly 25 years ago.

But even as a political matter, Trump might be advised to take the AI freakout seriously. Americans are worried — not necessarily about extinction, but that the new technology will take their jobs. And by rejecting voter concerns about data centers, the president is leaping onto the wrong side of yet another issue as the GOP braces for tough midterm elections.

But the president's blasé attitude to AI may be traced to a host of political, economic and personality traits that have unleashed turmoil across his two presidencies and that will shape his legacy.

Any signal that AI development may slow would almost certainly trigger a reaction on the markets. As his Iran war sticks Americans with high gas prices and record diesel costs, Trump can't afford any Wall Street turbulence that would hurt 401k accounts and check GDP growth.

He's also showing philosophical objections to a slowdown. His presidency has been about unleashing business to make money, not dialing it back.

Former White House AI czar David Sacks argued over the weekend that by expressing concerns about AI's destructive potential, industry titans were trying to pressure politicians and the public into creating their own "preferred" regulatory system.

Trump is taking a similar approach. "When, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?" the president wrote Monday.

Trump's governing style isn't a good fit for this deeply complex issue. He said this week that he's an AI user, but whether that goes beyond posting wild memes depicting himself as various superheroes is unclear. And he gets his news from the traveling printer of his aide Natalie Harp.

At the same time, there's a possibility that's often overlooked in the riotous Washington of the second Trump era: What if the president is going against the tide because he's right about a few things?

This would not be the first time that a new technology has triggered warnings of doom that don't play out. And some skeptics doubt alarmist talk from AI chiefs is genuine, suspecting that they are obliquely talking up the potential of their technology ahead of initial public offerings in the coming months.

And Trump has a serious point that even if the US slows AI development, China probably won't, which would give it a superpower advantage.

Plenty of Democrats feel the same way, including President Joe Biden's former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, who wrote in Foreign Affairs earlier this year that Washington "must up its game" in integrating AI across the military, warning that the US would lose leverage if it failed.

But Trump's vision of his own power and place in history also explain his behavior.

He posted on Monday that America would be fine because it had a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT." This might placate some supporters — but even if it's true, it's hardly a viable position. AI will be a generational issue long after he's left office, and Trump, as the incumbent president, has a responsibility to set an early course.

Trump critics might wonder whether his views are shaped by personal considerations, including his ownership of stocks exposed to AI, as disclosed in a recent financial filing. The White House insists his accounts are independently managed by third-party institutions. But ethical questions raised by administration officials regulating industries in which their personal wealth is deeply invested has been a constant shadow over the president's second term.

Trump's resistance to unpleasant truths is also at work.

He's never presented his presidency as a vehicle for confronting far-off threats or to tackle complex problems. He's used it to enact revenge against his enemies, to troll his political foes, to boost his own fame and to invade the psyches of billions of people across the globe.

Trump would never issue the kind of dialectical statement that his first predecessor, President Barack Obama, released on Tuesday. The 44th president said he'd been agonizing over AI for a decade and that it was time for top US leaders to convene a national conversation.

"Whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us," Obama wrote.

Some Americans might have hoped from similar from Trump. But he's a rebel and a backlash president. His anti-establishment credentials depend on being an outsider, not a unifier.

And Obama's path ultimately points to a US-led international coalition. Trump hates multinational altruism. "America First" is about doubling down on US power, not watering it down.

If Trump refuses to lead, will Congress step in?

There's no time for serious action before the midterms. But if AI explodes as a top campaign theme, it's likely to drive the legislative agenda of whoever controls the House and Senate next year. And if Republicans suffer a wipeout because of Trump's refusal to listen to voters, they may have an incentive to break with the president.

"I am the Hoax Buster, and I'm right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

This headline has been updated.

fullText:
US vice-president’s comments come as former Anthropic researcher revisits recent claim AI could destroy humanity

The US vice-president has dismissed calls for global regulation of AI safety risks, telling companies creating the most advanced models: “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop.”

In remarks addressed towards Dario Amodei, the co-founder of Anthropic who has called on Washington DC to coordinate control of AI systems, including with China, JD Vance said: “If you’re gonna create Frankenstein, don’t come to the government and say we need regulation.”

He said tech bosses should instead: “Look inward and accept that if you’re building Frankenstein, No 1, you should stop and No 2, when companies come to you and say: ‘We need the tools to fight back against Frankenstein,’ give them those tools.”

Vance was speaking at an AI summit in Los Angeles after a week of rising global concern at the risks to humanity posed by the prospect of the creation of an artificial superintelligence, a technology that does not yet exist.

Amodei on Saturday warned that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months.

Although many doubt that claim, it added fuel to the suggestion from Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, that there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within 10 years. He was responding to a researcher, Jacob Coxon, who quit Anthropic with a similar warning.

On Tuesday night, Coxon gave an amended prognosis: “I do think that if we go slower we can take risk to 0%, but this requires radical action.” He also admitted “it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios” in which AI kills all humans and said: “I need to work on communicating this point.”

Vance’s willingness to consider that AI could pose a real risk marked a split from the US president, Donald Trump, who wrote this week: “AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Trump posted on social media that AI is going to be “the greatest economic development engine in history – bigger than oil, gold, diamonds, or even the internet”.

Vance has said he suspects AI leaders of raising the alarm about safety risks as a “Trojan horse”. Amodei has proposed industry coordination to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” while US and global regulation is implemented. Critics of the companies believe they are encouraging the US government to create tough new rules – shaped in their interests – that could limit wider competition in a tactic known as regulatory capture.

OpenAI, which lost control of hundreds of AI agents during testing this summer which then conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website, said on Monday it was backing bipartisan efforts by lawmakers in Washington to address catastrophic risks from AI and it has been coordinating with Google and Anthropic.

On Wednesday, Reuters reported claims from an independent researcher, Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, that OpenAI’s rogue agents had started probing Hugging Face for weaknesses nearly two months before the attack.

Sam Altman, the Chat GPT-maker’s chief executive, on Tuesday criticised suggestions from other companies that “we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible”. Altman said: “There should be no qualifier on that.”

Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and chief executive of Meta, advocated that companies should take unilateral safety action. He said his company had recently delayed the release of its most recent AI model, Muse, “for several months to focus on safety and security”.

“We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

Meta has been forced to pay out billions in legal cases related to harms caused by its social media platforms. Last month it settled a case with US states claiming Facebook and Instagram harmed children by agreeing to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn).

Zuckerberg stressed: “[AI] labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”

title: Texas Republican's post on Asian Americans at UT Austin sparks accusations of racism
description: -Nuño WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A Republican nominee for a Texas office drew bipartisan criticism after posting a photo from a University of Texas football game that critics called
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - A Republican nominee for a Texas office drew bipartisan criticism after posting a photo from a University of Texas football game that critics called racist, portraying the Austin campus as dominated by foreign students contrary to enrollment data.

Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, drew a ‌sharp rebuke from fellow Republicans as well as Democrats after posting a crowd shot at a University of Texas football game, while suggesting that what appeared to be ‌students of South Asian descent reflected a large foreign-born or international student presence on campus.

"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French posted ​to his X account. He went on to claim that UT prioritizes foreign students in admissions and feared Texans were losing opportunities at the university.

"I weep for the families in Texas who can't get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans," he said.

But enrollment figures released by the University of Texas at Austin show international students account for less than 10% of the total student body. Total enrollment reached 55,000 students for the fall 2025 semester, including 5,140 international students. Texas residents make up 80.5% of all enrolled students.

For the undergraduate class, international students make up 4.3%, and a state law requires ‌90% of every incoming freshman class to be Texas residents. UT ⁠Austin automatically admits the top 5% of performers — who are also Texas residents — at every high school in the state.

The Texas legislature designed the initiative to promote diversity without explicitly considering race. As in most of the country, Texas high school students are separated by geography, income and demographics, and ⁠by guaranteeing admission to top students at each high school, the statewide policy helps ensure universities draw from a broad cross-section of Texas communities.

That means more than 90% of students at UT Austin are domestic, and more than four out of every five are Texans.

Vedant Nair, 24, who graduated from UT in 2024, said his parents immigrated to Oklahoma in the 1990s from Mumbai so his father could pursue an MBA ​at ​Oklahoma State University. Nair was born in Oklahoma City and recalls running around in a child-size OSU Cowboys ​football helmet and driving a mini John Deere tractor. His upbringing, he ‌said, was no different than those of his fellow Texans after his family moved to Dallas in elementary school.

Attending UT Austin was a dream come true, and a normal, American experience, he said.

"If you stripped away my name and skin color, I think my story is pretty similar to a lot of other Texans at massive public high schools," Nair said. "The point is that myself, and all the other kids in that picture, are just regular American kids."

University spokespeople and French did not respond to a request for comment.

The debate touches on a broader political argument that non-U.S. citizens are "displacing" American students at elite public universities, and the country at large.

French's remarks drew criticism from political figures and other social media users, who characterized the posts as racist or xenophobic.

Rodney ‌Coates, a sociology professor at Miami University in Ohio, said French's comments echoed longstanding anti-immigrant and anti-Asian narratives ​in the U.S. that have historically portrayed minority groups as threats to opportunities for others.

"It's easier to come up ​with a racist argument to organize a group of people under the presumption that, ​hey, they're hurting your chances," Coates said. Such appeals often have little to do with the people being targeted and instead seek to mobilize voters ‌by portraying them as victims. "Hate is one of the easiest means of ​organizing," he said.

University figures show white students made up ​about 31.5% of enrollment in 2024 to 2025, Hispanic students 25.5% and Asian students 22.4%.

University reporting treats race and ethnicity separately from international student status, meaning most students categorized as Asian are U.S. citizens or permanent residents rather than international students.

The image French shared was a screenshot from a video posted by the official athletics account at UT Austin. He did ​not include information identifying the citizenship, immigration status, residency or enrollment ‌status of any individuals shown.

For Nair, the unfortunate part of French's post was that it criticized a high point in school-pride history: the football team defeated The ​Ohio State University, the No. 1-ranked football team in the country.

"I don't think there is anything more American than people in cowboy hats yelling their heads off ​after one of the greatest comeback wins in college football history," he said.

Sept 15 (Reuters) - Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday the U.S. acknowledgement that Washington had deployed orbital weapons ignored the ‌possible consequences of a conflict and threatened long-term stability ‌in space-based activity.

"In pursuit of its narrow self-interests, Washington is ready to completely ignore ​the catastrophic consequences for humanity of any armed conflict in orbit," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a commentary on the ministry website.

Zakharova said the presence of U.S. weapons in space risks the prospects ‌for space exploration.

"Colossal risks ⁠are created for numerous socio-economic processes on Earth and people's well-being directly depends on them," she said.

U.S. ⁠Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a conference near Washington, D.C., on Monday that the United States possessed "on-orbit space control weapons capable of ​defending ​the Joint Force against hostile adversary ​action."

The statement was the ‌strongest admission by a U.S. official of American weapons in space amid rising space tensions with Russia and China.

Zakharova described the acknowledgement as part of attempts to "distract world attention from the U.S.' own aggressive strivings in terms of space," including "absurd" accusations that Moscow was ‌developing anti-satellite weapons.

"The moratorium on testing ... ​anti-satellite missiles promoted by the so-called 'collective West' ​is laden with hypocrisy, ​as in reality it does not affect the use ‌of weapons that the U.S. already ​has and does ​not apply to other types of anti-satellite systems that Washington is seeking to develop," she said.

Zakharova said resolutions co-authored by ​Russia on barring deployment ‌of space-based weapons and transparency in using space would ​be presented to the U.N. General Assembly next month.

(Reporting ​by Reuters; Editing by Rod Nickel)

title: Houthi advances leave Trump with only bad choices
description: Washington appears loath to step into another front as new oil disruptions send prices soaring.
fullText:
The Trump administration is running out of good options in the Middle East after Iranian-backed Houthi militants seized more strategic territory — and further squeezed world energy markets.

The administration could join the fray after Yemeni forces, supported by Saudi Arabia, failed to repel the Houthis' capture of the Red Sea port of Mokha and three islands key to controlling the waterway.

Or the White House could leave the region to sort out the Houthis alone, and bear the pain of oil prices that spiraled up to $109 a barrel Monday. The spike was caused by both the choking of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait passageway to the Red Sea and the closure of a critical Saudi Arabian oil pipeline following an attack Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

Neither policy choice for the U.S. is terribly appealing, and one Arab diplomat in the region sensed inaction from the U.S., or "a kind of disregard."

"They feel they don't want to go into any conflict in the region besides Iran despite the fact it is a strategic setback to the U.S.," added the diplomat, who, like others, was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive security issues.

In response to questions on the Houthi attack, a senior administration official sent POLITICO talking points it had first sent in mid-August, before the current escalation.

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges," the official said both Monday and on Aug. 19.

The recycled statement also mentioned the U.S. expects the Houthis to observe the terms of a ceasefire reached last year that saw the rebel group agree to stop attacking American ships in exchange for the U.S. ending a bombing campaign against the Houthis that had hit at least 800 targets in Yemen.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday "we've been in constant contact with the Emiratis, the Saudis and others who are affected in the region," and added "we've also been engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis themselves."

Officially, the U.S. maintains its strong military ties with Saudi Arabia. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Monday in Jeddah, according to Saudi state media. The two discussed "regional security cooperation," according to CENTCOM public affairs.

But the appetite for more warfare seems limited throughout Washington. "Oil is already over $100 a barrel, and there's no end in sight to these price fluctuations until the Trump Administration negotiates an end to this war," said Senate Foreign Relations ranking member Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.), a member of SFRC, said, "It is vital that the United States and our regional allies work together to maintain an open flow of trade through Middle East shipping lanes." He didn't answer whether the U.S. should get involved in strikes against the Houthis.

The tepid response in Washington may also stem from whiplash after the Houthis made dramatic advances in a matter of hours, evading both Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and the Saudi and U.S. militaries. One exasperated person in the region called it "a Saudi-American f**k up of epic proportions," CNN's Nic Robertson and Lauren Kent reported.

The White House and Saudi Arabia's embassy didn't immediately confirm an Axios report that MBS asked the U.S. for help in striking the Houthis. Yemen's embassy also didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Arab diplomat said that Yemen has asked the U.S. to restart its support of Yemen's armed forces and humanitarian programs. The diplomat said Saudi Arabia was also trying to draw the White House's attention.

"The idea of accepting the Houthis controlling strategic locations in Yemen is establishing a permanent national security crisis for Saudi Arabia," the diplomat said.

A meeting of Gulf states and Iran, scheduled for Monday in Oman, was postponed due to what Iranian Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei described as a demand from Saudi Arabia.

Both Saudi Arabia and the government of Yemen are striking the Houthis, but "I don't see those as decisive moves," said Allison Minor, who served as the deputy special envoy for Yemen in the Biden administration and director for Arabian Peninsula affairs at the National Security Council under the first Trump administration. "It feels like we're gearing up for a protracted conflict," she added.

Michael Ratney, who served as U.S. ambassador to Riyadh under President Joe Biden, argued Gulf states would aim to make their own arrangements to cool the chaos.

"There will be a lot of diplomacy on this topic but we, the U.S., will not be the center of it," he said.

Ratney noted Saudi Arabia might be cautious about patching up its pipeline while active battle continues, which could keep fuel costly.

"The markets are starting to price in all the political risk that's going to be involved," he said.

fullText:
KYIV, Sept 14 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support a U.S. proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on ‌energy sites only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to ‌end its war on Ukraine.

Zelenskiy made his comments in his nightly video address after U.S. President Donald ​Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.

"If this can become the first de-escalatory step, a step towards ending Russian strikes against our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response, Ukraine is ready to support ‌de-escalation," Zelenskiy said.

"So far, no ⁠one has seen any genuine willingness on Russia's part to bring the war to an end. But if our American partners ⁠can secure Russia's genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps."

fullText:
Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI

China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule.

The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge.

Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”.

China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday.

In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.

Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China.

While Beijing rejects its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China, Xi Jinping, warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”.

But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power.

The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”.

Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity.

While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI, Donald Trump has dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of AI growth were raised.

The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September.

In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China.

“The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,” it said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Community holds vigil for missing DC mother a week after she disappeared, her phones, wallet, car and dog left behind
description: A terrified family is pleading for help in finding a woman who has been missing for more than a week after she disappeared from her Washington, DC, home without her phones, wallet or car.
fullText:
A terrified family is pleading for help in finding a woman who has been missing for more than a week after she disappeared from her Washington, DC, home without her phones, wallet or car.

Antoinette Forbes, 53, a single mother of a young boy and a beloved sister, was last seen in person Friday, September 4, in the 3200 block of Nebraska Avenue NW, according to the Metropolitan Police Department, which has released a missing-person poster seeking the public's help.

Police haven't released any information about her son.

Forbes is an Asian woman, 5 feet 2 inches tall and about 115 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes, police have said. Her clothing at the time is unknown.

Her family and friends say the circumstances of her disappearance are deeply alarming: Forbes' two phones, wallet, laptop and car were all left behind at her home, along with her dog, Max. The front door was unlocked.

"We're in absolute shock and horror," Forbes' older sister, Aileen Forbes, told CNN on Thursday. "We have our own very close-knit immediate family, but we have a very large extended family. We're horrified."

An investigation is active, police told CNN, declining to share further details.

Elizabeth Northrup, a friend of Forbes' with whom Aileen is staying as they search for her sister, told CNN they do not believe Forbes left her home voluntarily.

"(Law enforcement) certainly checked all the hospitals. We also have had friends check hospitals. She has not flown," Northrup said. "She did not walk out of that house and go voluntarily."

About a half-million people were reported missing last year in the United States, including those who may have left voluntarily, missing minors, kidnapping victims and others, according to the FBI's Crime Information Center.

Deciding how to proceed with searching for a missing person varies case to case, and sometimes race and news coverage play a role.

In the search for Antoinette Forbes, Aileen is holding onto hope and refuses to dwell on the worst-case scenarios, she said.

"I am trying really hard not to even conceive of that … because it would mean that my family is destroyed," she said. "I'm still trying very hard to keep the faith and the strong, harsh belief that I've had from the start that my sister is alive."

Friends, family and supporters of Forbes gathered for a vigil Saturday night at National Presbyterian Church in Washington, DC, marking one week since her disappearance. Loved ones came together "in a show of love, strength and hope for her safe return," according to a flyer about the vigil.

Alison Williams, who said she has known Forbes for nearly 30 years, told CNN affiliate WJLA the disappearance has been harrowing.

"I know so many other families have gone through similar experiences. It doesn't change how difficult it is, not only for her friends, but especially for her family who are so desperate to see her back," she said.

Just days before Antoinette Forbes was reported missing, the sisters had spoken on the phone as usual on weekend mornings, Aileen said.

She FaceTimed her sister on Saturday morning. They talked about their weekend and the week ahead — an ordinary conversation between two sisters who were especially close, she told CNN.

They planned to talk again the next day, but Aileen never heard from her, she said. As the days passed without contact, the family grew increasingly concerned. Aileen said she knew something was wrong when she reached out to her sister to tell her she had Covid-19 and did not receive a response.

"She's a very busy woman. She's got a full life," Aileen said. "Single mother, highly successful professional."

Forbes works as the associate vice president and head of public affairs at Eli Lilly, an American multinational pharmaceutical company, according to her LinkedIn page. The company is supporting police efforts to find her and encouraged anyone with information to contact police, a spokesperson told CNN.

"We are deeply concerned for Antoinette and are thinking of her and her family in this uncertain time," the spokesperson said. "We hope for her safe return."

But above all, Aileen said, her sister is a mother of a 10-year-old boy.

"(He) is Antoinette's life," Aileen said. "Antoinette is a 100% solid, reliable, intelligent, competent woman who is a devoted mother. She would never leave her son. She wouldn't leave her dog. She wouldn't leave her sister who needs her."

After days went by without a word, Aileen alerted family friends, Louis and Margarita, who live near Forbes' home and have a key, to check on her, she said. That was Monday, Labor Day.

Margarita texted Aileen after entering the home.

"I think something happened," the message said, according to Aileen.

"My heart stopped after I read that text," she said. Louis then called and described what they found.

Inside, according to her friends and family, were Forbes' two phones, including her work phone. So were her wallet and her laptop. Her car was in the driveway. Her dog, Max, was also at the house.

Police declined to say whether Forbes' home had surveillance cameras and whether investigators had reviewed any footage from the home or canvassed neighbors for video.

For Aileen, the waiting has become its own kind of torment.

"Today it's getting harder," she said. "We're getting later into the week, and some of the dark reality is hitting me."

But Forbes' friends and family are not ready to give up hope, and they are asking anyone who may have seen something – however small – to come forward.

"We need to know what happened," Aileen told CNN. "Someone had to have seen something, anything, some small thing, seen her. We need the evidence that's going to enable the police to do their jobs and bring Antoinette home."

The police department is asking anyone with information about Forbes' whereabouts to call 202-727-9099 or text 50411.

Rachel Clark, who says she has known Forbes for 13 years, shared a Facebook post appealing for help in finding her, saying those who love Forbes "are doing everything we can to keep her name, her face and her story in front of as many people as possible."

"She is brilliant, hilarious, feisty, fiercely loyal, and the kind of person who shows up for the people she loves," Clark wrote alongside photos of Forbes.

Clark told CNN she misses her friend and is "eager to bring her home."

In her post, Clark urged the public to look at photographs of Forbes and to contact police with any information that could help locate her.

"Antoinette, there are so many people looking for you and fighting for you," Clark wrote in the Facebook post.

"We love you. We miss you. And we will not stop until you are home."

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Cleveland Browns DC Mike Rutenberg: ‘We’re arriving with bad intentions’
description: Cleveland new man in charge of the defense has a clear idea of what he wants from his side of the ball.
fullText:
The Cleveland Browns will sport a new defensive look when they take the field on Sunday for their Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Some of those changes are by design: defensive end Jared Verse replaces Myles Garrett, linebacker Quincy Williams replaces Devin Bush, and defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg takes over for Jim Schwartz.

There were some unexpected changes, however, most notably along the defensive line, after defensive end Alex Wright, who was expected to be a starter, was lost for the season to a torn Achilles tendon.

That led general manager Andrew Berry to bring in veterans Sam Williams and Derek Barnett, and Rutenberg to experiment with Michael Hall Jr. at defensive end.

Rutenberg had his weekly press conference on Thursday and addressed several topics. Here are four takeaways from what he had to say.

There are no bigger shoes to fill for a defensive player than those of Myles Garrett, who picked up his second Defensive Player of the Year Award in 2025 after bagging an NFL-record 23 sacks.

Garrett is now with the Los Angeles Rams, while Verse is in Cleveland and bringing his own style to the defense, according to Rutenberg:

"(Jared's) such a unique guy. He's really like a unicorn in that he sets a standard with his play style and who he is. Really, what we saw early is what we continue to get. He sets that standard from the jump, in meetings, great questions, great insight. And then on the practice field, his standard of not only performance but style, and how hard he plays, has been the same every day. It's really cool to see."

Adding veterans is nice, especially for a team that is in the second year of a youth movement, but adding them so close to the start of the season is not always ideal. Especially with everyone on the defense already working with a new defensive coordinator and not necessarily able to quickly bring the new guys up to speed.

But so far everything has gone smoothly with Barnett and Williams, according to Rutenberg:

"It's awesome to get new guys. The nature of this league is that you get new players, and those guys have worked as hard as you could possibly imagine. They've worked their butts off. Derek's obviously been in it. Sam's had experience in it. Those guys are pros, man. They approach it the right way. We've got a great defensive line coaching staff, starting with Jacques (Cesaire), Ralph (Street), Laroy (Reynolds), Shaq (Wilson), and together they're preparing really hard. It's really cool to see."

finding a way to win on defense@GetSpectrum | #DawgPound pic.twitter.com/pREF2cg2NZ

All through training camp and the preseason, Rutenberg has talked about how "the ball is oxygen," and the defense needs it to survive. He also wants his defense to have a very particular mindset when it takes the field:

"When the ball is thrown, we're arriving with bad intentions. We're built off that. We choose violence in everything we do, and it doesn't have to be a tackle; ball's in the air, we're knocking it out. That's what we're built off. We do our job so my brother can do his; I do mine and a little bit more. And our guys have done that. They do it in practice; they do it in walk-through. It's awesome to see.

"I'm excited to watch us play as hard as possible. I can't wait just to watch us celebrate together. I can't wait to see our preparation hopefully come to life. We're built off violence, and that's what we're looking for in every play."

Far too often, fans and media focus on sacks and turnovers as the only sign that a defense is successful. Those are fun, no doubt, but pressuring a quarterback into a bad throw is just as helpful. And turnovers are not something that a defense can control.

For Rutenberg, however, there is only one clear goal:

"Win. Win. I want to help the Browns win. I learned that from Jeff Ulbrich, man. Raheem Morris used to say, 'help the team win on defense. Find a way to help the team win on defense.' It's a team game; we're a team staff, Browns helping Browns, man. I want to help this team win."

title: Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
description: Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined Washington Spirit from Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football - and possibly one that sets a world record.
fullText:
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.

The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.

Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.

BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.

The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.

Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.

If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.

However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.

With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.

Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.

She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.

The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.

London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.

Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.

When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.

"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."

Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.

"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."

Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.

She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.

Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.

Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.

"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.

There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.

Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.

Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.

Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.

She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.

For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Prediction markets tracking this year's U.S. congressional elections are "extremely vulnerable" to manipulation as their forecasts can shift on even comparatively small-dollar wagers, ‌according to research published on Wednesday.

The findings from the non-profit research group ‌Anti-Corruption Data Collective are likely to amplify concerns from Democrats and consumer advocates that betting on political races ​jeopardizes public confidence in the electoral system by potentially casting doubt on outcomes or encouraging insider trading.

Representatives for Kalshi and Polymarket, which currently dominate the U.S. prediction market industry, rejected the findings, however, saying Wednesday that market forces created a financial incentive to correct distorted prices ‌by encouraging punters to wager ⁠on the better likelihood.

The booming prediction market industry allows users to bet on the outcomes of virtually anything, including sports, war, drug trials ⁠and elections. Proponents often say the probabilities such markets indicate amount to valuable forecasts, with multiple major media outlets citing market odds in their coverage.

According to the report, for example, ​in more than ​11,000 of the markets tracking congressional races this year ​across Kalshi, Polymarket and Polymarket's U.S. ‌platform, virtually all, or 94%, would see a movement equivalent to 10% in probability following a single bet of less than $1,000. In hundreds of cases on Polymarket, the report said, markets retained their new level for 24 hours and typically did so for around four days.

ACDC researcher Michelle Kendler-Kretsch said political prediction markets attracted large dollar volumes ‌not motivated by short-term profits, which undermined the ​prediction markets' claims to accuracy.

"The conditions for accuracy are ​not being met in markets about ​the November midterms and primaries," she said in a statement.

A Kalshi ‌representative said to the contrary that a ​recent company case ​study showed that, even after a trader had poured more than $1 million into a market concerning former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, "prices corrected in just nine ​seconds."

A Polymarket spokesperson likewise ‌said that mispriced odds spelled opportunity for other traders: "They are incentivized to get the ​price back to what you would expect it to be."

Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners

The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.

“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.

The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.

Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.

“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”

It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.

But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.

Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.

“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

The program, currently unnamed but designated F/A-XX, has been buffeted by delays and funding disputes for years. Congress pushed back, earmarking $750 million for F/A-XX in the massive ⁠tax-cut and spending bill signed into law in 2025 and an additional $1.4 billion in fiscal 2026.

With China rapidly fielding advanced combat aircraft — including ones Beijing describes as ​sixth-generation — the ​stakes of further delay are high, ​leaving the Navy without a modern ‌fighter capable of operating from carriers in the 2030s and beyond, potentially undermining its ability to project power in contested environments, a U.S. official has said.
